title: Piezoelectricity
description: Electric charge generated in certain solids due to mechanical stress
wiki_lead:
Piezoelectricity (, US: ) is the electric charge that accumulates in certain solid materials—such as crystals, certain ceramics, and biological matter such as bone, DNA, and various proteins—in response to applied mechanical stress.
The piezoelectric effect results from the linear electromechanical interaction between the mechanical and electrical states in crystalline materials with no inversion symmetry. The piezoelectric effect is a reversible process:  materials exhibiting the piezoelectric effect  also exhibit the reverse piezoelectric effect, the internal generation of a mechanical strain resulting from an applied electric field. For example, lead zirconate titanate crystals will generate measurable piezoelectricity when their static structure is deformed by about 0.1% of the original dimension. Conversely, those same crystals will change about 0.1% of their static dimension when an external electric field is applied. The inverse piezoelectric effect is used in the production of ultrasound waves.
French physicists Jacques and Pierre Curie discovered piezoelectricity in 1880. The piezoelectric effect is exploited in many forms, including the production and detection of sound, piezoelectric inkjet printing, generation of high voltage electricity, as a clock generator in electronic devices, in microbalances, to drive an ultrasonic nozzle, and in ultrafine focusing of optical assemblies. It forms the basis for scanning probe microscopes that resolve images at the scale of atoms. It is used in the pickups of some electronically amplified guitars and as triggers in most modern electronic drums. The piezoelectric effect also finds everyday uses, such as generating sparks to ignite gas cooking and heating devices, torches, and cigarette lighters.

Etymology
The word piezoelectricity means electricity resulting from pressure. It is derived from Ancient Greek  πιέζω (piézō) 'to squeeze or press' and  ἤλεκτρον (ḗlektron) 'amber' (an ancient source of static electricity).  The German form of the word (Piezoelektrizität) was coined in 1881 by the German physicist Wilhelm Gottlieb Hankel; the English word was derived from German in 1883.


History


Discovery and early research

The pyroelectric effect, by which a material generates an electric potential in response to a temperature change, was studied by Carl Linnaeus and Franz Aepinus in the mid-18th century. Drawing on this knowledge, both René Just Haüy and Antoine César Becquerel posited a relationship between mechanical stress and electric charge; however, experiments by both proved inconclusive.

The first demonstration of the direct piezoelectric effect was in 1880 by the brothers Pierre Curie and Jacques Curie. grok_lead: Piezoelectricity is the reversible electromechanical phenomenon in which certain non-centrosymmetric crystalline materials generate an electric charge when subjected to mechanical stress (direct piezoelectric effect) and, conversely, undergo mechanical deformation when an electric field is applied (converse piezoelectric effect). This effect arises from the displacement of charged ions within the crystal lattice, leading to a net electric polarization without requiring external charge carriers. The direct piezoelectric effect was discovered in 1880 by French physicists Pierre Curie and Jacques Curie, who observed it in crystals such as quartz, tourmaline, and Rochelle salt while studying the pressure-induced electrification of solids. The converse effect was theoretically predicted in 1881 by Gabriel Lippmann based on thermodynamic principles and experimentally confirmed shortly thereafter by the Curie brothers. These discoveries laid the foundation for understanding piezoelectricity as a linear coupling between mechanical and electrical properties in materials lacking a center of symmetry in their unit cell. Common piezoelectric materials include natural crystals like quartz and synthetic ones such as lead zirconate titanate (PZT) ceramics, polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) polymers, and relaxor ferroelectrics like lead magnesium niobate (PMN), which exhibit enhanced sensitivity due to nanoscale structural disorder. PZT, for instance, is prized for its high piezoelectric coefficients, enabling efficient energy conversion, while PMN relaxors can be over 100% more responsive to mechanical stimuli than traditional ferroelectrics like PZT. Piezoelectricity finds widespread applications in sensors, actuators, transducers, and energy harvesters, powering devices from ultrasound imaging systems and sonar to microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) in consumer electronics and vibrational energy converters in wearable technology. In civil engineering, it supports structural health monitoring and vibration damping, while in biomedical fields, it enables precise actuators for microscopy and implantable devices. Ongoing research focuses on lead-free alternatives and nanomaterials to improve performance and sustainability in these diverse fields.
